summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base that extends the Entity MIB with information about the state of physical entities. It also defines textual conventions that represent various states, intended to be imported by other MIB modules. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Network gear has parts that are on, off, or broken. This memo gives a standard way to ask a device what state each part is in.

questions: what is the entity state mib
what is hot standby versus cold standby in snmp
how do i read the alarm state of a physical entity
subtitle: A standard SNMP table that reports whether each physical part of a device is locked, working, busy, alarmed or on standby.

tldr.problem: The Entity MIB lists the physical parts of a managed device, but it gives no standard way to ask what state each part is in: permitted, working, in use, alarmed or standing by.
tldr.mechanism: The Entity State MIB adds a table with one row per reporting entity, with objects for administrative, operational, usage, alarm and standby state, plus a last-changed time. It also defines reusable textual conventions for those states and two notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. Other MIB modules can import its state types instead of inventing their own.

today: RFC 4268 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Entity MIB in RFC 4133.

sections.title: Why Physical Entities Need State
sections.content:
RFC 4268 extends the Entity MIB (RFC 4133) with information about the state of physical entities. It is a MIB module written in SMIv2 and is normally read through SNMP. The terms "state" and "status" are used interchangeably in the memo.

The goal is to define a useful subset of the state attributes that could be tracked for an entity. The subset must fit state models such as the one in the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863) and reuse existing, well-deployed models. The table is a subset of the ISO/OSI states also defined in ITU X.731.

The memo also defines a set of textual conventions for the states. The intent is that other MIB modules import them rather than define their own representations.
sections.eli5: Network gear is made of many parts. This memo gives everyone the same words for what condition a part is in, so the answers look the same on every device.

sections.title: The Five Kinds of State
sections.content:
Five kinds of state are tracked for each entity.

  • Administrative state is permission to use the entity or a prohibition against using it, imposed through management services.
  • Operational state says whether the entity is physically installed and working. Unlike ifOperStatus in the Interfaces MIB, it is independent of the administrative state.
  • Usage state says whether the entity is in use right now and, if so, whether it has spare capacity for more users. It refers to the entity's ability to service other entities in its containment hierarchy.
  • Alarm state says whether alarms are active against the entity. Beyond the X.731 states it adds warning and indeterminate, to map more completely to the Alarm MIB (RFC 3877).
  • Standby state says whether the entity is hot standby, cold standby or currently providing service.

All state objects in the memo are raw state: the state of the entity independent of its parents and children in the containment hierarchy. The alternative, computed state, is influenced by the states of those related entities and is not what this MIB reports.
sections.eli5: Each part gets five questions: is it allowed to work, is it working, is it busy, is anything wrong, and is it a spare? Each answer is about that part alone, not about the parts around it.

sections.title: The Entity State Table
sections.content:
The module is ENTITY-STATE-MIB, placed at { mib-2 131 }. Its main object is entStateTable, a sparse augment of the entPhysicalTable. Rows are indexed by entPhysicalIndex, and a row appears only for physical classes that can report at least some of the state in the table.

Each row has six objects: entStateLastChanged, entStateAdmin, entStateOper, entStateUsage, entStateAlarm and entStateStandby. The first is a DateAndTime recording when any of the other five last changed. If nothing has changed since local system re-initialization it holds the initialization time, and if nothing has changed since the entity was added it holds the insertion time.

Only entStateAdmin is read-write. The rest are read-only. The memo makes no effort to standardize how entities in a physical class behave, only how their state is reported, so each description says how to behave when an entity cannot support part of a state. For example, an entity that cannot operate in a standby role always reports providingService.
sections.eli5: There is one row for each part. Each row holds the five answers and a note of when any of them last changed. You can only change the first answer, the permission, and the others are read-only.

sections.title: The State Types
sections.content:
The module ENTITY-STATE-TC-MIB, at { mib-2 130 }, defines five textual conventions.

  • EntityAdminState: unknown, locked, shuttingDown, unlocked. Shutting down means usage is limited to current instances of use.
  • EntityOperState: unknown, disabled, enabled, testing. Enabled means partially or fully operable, and disabled means totally inoperable.
  • EntityUsageState: unknown, idle, active, busy. Idle means no users, active means in use with spare capacity, and busy means in use with none.
  • EntityAlarmStatus: a set of bits (BITS) rather than a single value.
  • EntityStandbyStatus: unknown, hotStandby, coldStandby, providingService. A hot standby can take over immediately, while a cold standby needs some initialization first.

Because the alarm status is a bit string, several conditions can be set at once. The bits are unknown, underRepair, critical, major, minor, warning and indeterminate. If no bits are set, no active alarms are known and the entity is not under repair. The warning and indeterminate bits are not defined in X.733.

The memo points out that unknown (no ability to report that state) differs from indeterminate (alarms exist but their severity is not known).
sections.eli5: Most answers come from a short menu, like a light that is red, yellow or green. The alarm answer is a row of checkboxes, so several problems can be ticked at the same time.

sections.title: Rules, Notifications and Links to Other MIBs
sections.content:
Some rules matter for how the objects behave. Setting entStateAdmin to a value the entity's administrative model does not support gives an inconsistentValue error. If an implementation cannot accurately report entStateOper while entStateAdmin is anything other than unlocked, entStateOper MUST be unknown. The alarm object does not include alarms raised on child components. Usage state supports only direct containment, while the other states use all three definitions of the entity's user (direct containment, anywhere in the hierarchy, or a means outside the MIB).

Two notifications are defined, entStateOperEnabled and entStateOperDisabled. An agent sends one when it detects that entStateOper for one of its entities has moved into that state. Each carries entStateAdmin and entStateAlarm, and the entity is identified from the entPhysicalIndex in a variable binding.

The memo also maps its states to older MIBs. An ifAdminStatus of up equals an entStateAdmin of unlocked, and an ifOperStatus of up equals an entStateOper of enabled. The Bridge MIB's dot1dStpPortEnable maps to locked or unlocked for port entities, and hrDeviceStatus in the Host Resources MIB maps to entStateOper values. Alarm details are found by searching alarmActiveTable in the Alarm MIB for the matching entPhysicalIndex.
sections.eli5: When a part switches between working and not working, the device can send a message saying so, along with its permission and any alarms. The memo also explains how its answers match the older ones that other MIBs already gave.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content: A system that claims compliance with entStateCompliance MUST support the mandatory group entStateGroup, which holds all six table objects. The notification group entStateNotificationsGroup is optional. Write access to entStateAdmin is not required, since the compliance statement lowers its minimum access to read-only.
sections.eli5: A device must be able to answer all the questions. Sending messages about changes is optional, and so is letting someone change the permission.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The textual conventions module defines no management objects, so the memo says it has no impact on the security of the Internet. The main concern is entStateAdmin, the one read-write object. Setting it to locked or shuttingDown can disrupt services, from those on one port to those on a whole device. Access to it should be protected.

Even read-only access is sensitive. The objects reveal which resources in a network are active and which are on standby, and this can be used to optimize attacks.

The memo RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Being able to lock a part could switch off something important, and knowing which parts are spares helps a bad guy plan. So only trusted people should be able to use these controls.

items.title: entStateAdmin
items.text: Permission to use the entity: unknown, locked, shuttingDown, unlocked.

items.title: entStateOper
items.text: Installed and working: unknown, disabled, enabled, testing.

items.title: entStateUsage
items.text: In use or not: unknown, idle, active, busy.

items.title: entStateAlarm
items.text: Active alarms, as a set of bits.
